neurological_exam.additional: COMPLEX DIAGNOSTIC PICTURE: (1) Heavy alcohol use: 4-6 drinks/day — this alone can cause behavioral changes, cerebellar signs, and dementia; (2) Non-adherent CPAP for moderate-severe OSA — sleep-disordered breathing impairs cognition; (3) Depression history — could be early FTD misdiagnosed; (4) Suspicious employment termination for 'compliance violations' — possibly FTD-related judgment impairment leading to rule-breaking behavior; (5) Family history concerning for FTD. The cerebellar signs (intention tremor, wide base, impaired tandem) likely represent alcoholic cerebellar degeneration. The behavioral syndrome, however, has features beyond what alcohol alone would explain.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change, impaired judgment, grandiosity — 2 years (wife-reported)
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W is a 62-year-old former financial advisor who presents with his wife after being referred by his internist for cognitive evaluation. His wife describes a 2-year history of progressive personality changes that have been difficult to separate from his escalating alcohol use. He was terminated from his financial advisory position 18 months ago following several compliance violations — he had been making unauthorized trades in client accounts and dismissing colleagues' concerns about policy violations with dismissive and sometimes belligerent responses. He has never acknowledged that these violations were his fault, insisting he was 'unfairly targeted.' Prior to this, he had a 28-year career without any disciplinary record. At home, he has become increasingly impulsive — making a $30,000 investment in a scheme his wife considers fraudulent, and responding with rage when questioned. He now drinks 4-6 drinks daily by his report; his wife estimates 8-10. He has become grandiose, making claims about his business acumen that are not consistent with his recent performance. He has lost empathy — when his son had a significant health scare, he expressed no concern. He has become highly perseverative in arguments — repeating the same accusations against his former employer in every conversation for 18 months. His sleep apnea is moderate-severe and he abandoned his CPAP after two weeks. He has a family history of possible dementia in his mother (onset her late 50s) and possible psychiatric institutionalization in his maternal uncle. The diagnostic complexity involves separating alcohol-related cognitive impairment (which is real and contributing to cerebellar signs) from an underlying neurodegenerative process that may have predated or precipitated the escalating alcohol use. In some FTD patients, disinhibited behavior and loss of social control manifest first as substance misuse, which then obscures the underlying diagnosis.

mri.impression: Moderate bilateral frontal atrophy with disproportionate volume loss compared to posterior cortex and temporal lobes. The degree of frontal atrophy appears disproportionate to the cerebellar and white matter changes that can be attributed to alcohol alone, raising concern for primary frontotemporal pathology with concurrent alcoholic cerebellar degeneration. FDG-PET is essential to characterize the frontal metabolic pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Severe bilateral frontal hypometabolism. Orbitofrontal cortex, medial prefrontal, anterior cingulate, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex show 28-36% FDG reduction versus cerebellar reference. Note: after 2-week sobriety, acute alcohol effect on FDG-PET has resolved — persistent hypometabolism reflects structural/degenerative change.
Moderate bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism (18-22% reduction).
PRESERVED posterior cingulate and parietal cortex — no posterior cingulate sign.
Mildly reduced cerebellar FDG uptake consistent with alcoholic cerebellar degeneration — used as reference with caution; supplemented with occipital normalization for frontal ratios.

output.impression: Severe bilateral frontotemporal hypometabolism with preserved posterior cortex, obtained after 2-week sobriety period to eliminate acute alcohol effect. This degree of frontal hypometabolism is greater than can be attributed to alcohol-related frontal damage alone at this level of use, and is consistent with primary bvFTD. The preservation of posterior cingulate excludes Alzheimer's disease.

interactions: Naltrexone (alcohol use disorder treatment): hepatic metabolism — mildly elevated liver enzymes do not contraindicate; monthly injections preferred for adherence in bvFTD
Sertraline for bvFTD behavioral symptoms: minimal alcohol interaction; may help disinhibition
contraindications: Disulfiram: avoid in bvFTD — patient may lack impulse control to avoid alcohol, leading to dangerous disulfiram-alcohol reaction
Benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal: use with caution in bvFTD — can worsen cognition; use structured CIWA protocol with medical supervision
warnings: Alcohol cessation is CRITICAL — alcohol is actively worsening cerebellar and frontal function AND masking FTD evaluation
Continued alcohol use may prevent meaningful clinical trial eligibility
Thiamine supplementation: oral thiamine 100 mg TID for prophylaxis given low-normal thiamine and heavy alcohol use
alternatives: Inpatient detoxification may be necessary given dependency level
Family-focused alcohol counseling — wife must understand alcohol cessation is part of FTD treatment

output.query: bvFTD alcohol use disorder disinhibition misdiagnosis overlap

results.title: Alcohol use disorder preceding bvFTD diagnosis: a diagnostic challenge

output.summary: In bvFTD, disinhibition and loss of social control can manifest first as escalating alcohol use, which may precede formal FTD diagnosis by years. The FTD-related frontal disinhibition removes the ability to self-regulate drinking behavior, leading to escalating alcohol misuse as an early behavioral symptom. Key clinical implication: in a middle-aged patient whose alcohol use is escalating in conjunction with new behavioral disinhibition and social dysfunction, FTD must be considered in the differential even when alcohol use disorder is prominent. Alcohol-related frontal damage alone typically requires 10-20 years of heavy use to produce the degree of frontal atrophy seen in this patient. FDG-PET obtained after sobriety period helps distinguish alcohol-related from primary FTD metabolic changes.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia — sporadic — with concurrent alcohol use disorder and alcoholic cerebellar degeneration

differential.key_feature: Cerebellar degeneration and liver enzyme elevation are alcohol-related; however, degree of frontal atrophy and frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism after sobriety period exceeds what alcohol alone explains at this level of use; normal thiamine and mammillary bodies exclude Wernicke-Korsakoff
Amyloid PET negative; FDG-PET shows frontotemporal pattern without posterior cingulate sign; hippocampi relatively preserved

differential.diagnosis: Frontal lobe syndrome from alcohol alone
differential.key_feature: FDG-PET obtained after 2-week sobriety still shows severe (28-36%) frontal hypometabolism — persistent beyond acute alcohol effect; degree of frontal atrophy disproportionate to alcohol use history

Grandiosity and disinhibition in bipolar occur in the context of mood elevation; this patient has persistent (not episodic) disinhibition and loss of empathy with progressive course and structural frontal atrophy

critical_actions: Thiamine must be supplemented immediately in heavy alcohol user — do not wait for level to fall below normal range
FDG-PET should be obtained after sobriety period (minimum 2 weeks) to distinguish alcohol-related metabolic changes from primary FTD hypometabolism
Disulfiram is contraindicated in bvFTD — impaired impulse control and judgment mean patient cannot reliably avoid alcohol
contraindicated_actions: Disulfiram in bvFTD patient — contraindicated due to disinhibition making alcohol avoidance unreliable and dangerous disulfiram-alcohol reaction possible
key_reasoning_points: Alcohol use disorder in bvFTD can be a SYMPTOM of the frontal disinhibition — the escalating alcohol use may represent loss of frontal inhibitory control rather than primary addiction, which predated or precipitated FTD

FDG-PET should be obtained after a sobriety period in heavy alcohol users — acute alcohol effect reduces FDG uptake globally, masking specific FTD pattern; persistent frontotemporal hypometabolism after sobriety indicates primary pathology

The employment termination for 'compliance violations' is a classic early FTD presentation — frontal disinhibition leading to rule-breaking behavior at work without recognition of the transgression, years before formal cognitive testing abnormalities

red_herrings.data_point: Heavy alcohol use with elevated GGT, MCV, CDT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute entire syndrome to alcohol-related dementia
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Alcohol is a concurrent problem and contributes to cerebellar signs, but the frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism (after sobriety) and the degree of frontal atrophy exceed what alcohol alone explains — primary bvFTD with concurrent alcohol use disorder

red_herrings.intended_effect: Raise concern for ataxic syndrome (spinocerebellar ataxia, multiple system atrophy)
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Cerebellar atrophy on MRI with superior vermis predominance is the classic pattern of alcoholic cerebellar degeneration — not SCA or MSA; frontal syndrome is the primary FTD component

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD with concurrent alcohol use disorder. Key teaching: alcohol escalation may be a symptom of FTD disinhibition; FDG-PET after sobriety period isolates primary FTD changes; disulfiram contraindicated in FTD due to impaired impulse control.
